intro: The first time you hold a real chef's knife, it feels heavier and longer than anything you have used at the table. That is the right moment to learn how to hold it, because the habits you build in the first week are the ones your hands will keep. A knife does exactly what your hands tell it. This unit is about telling it clearly: where to put your thumb, how to tuck your fingertips, where the tip goes, and what to do with the knife when you are not cutting.

You will learn the parts of the knife and why a sharp one is safer than a dull one. You will practice the pinch grip and the claw until they feel normal, then the rocking cut that turns a carrot into even coins. You will set up a station that cannot slide, carry a knife across a room without anyone flinching, and wash and store it so the next person's hand is safe too.

Then the cuts. Slice, dice in three sizes, mince, julienne and chiffonade all have names because each one does a different job in a dish. You will dice an onion, mince garlic and roll basil into ribbons, and you will finish with a timed practical where the grade comes from safety, correct sizes, even pieces and a clean board. By the end you will be able to read a recipe's cutting words and do exactly what they ask.
bigQuestion: How do you handle a chef's knife so that every cut is safe, even and the size the recipe asks for?

test.q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a dull one?
choices: It cuts with little force, so it does not slip

at the end of the handle

a fist on top of the food

test.why: Tip down, handle rocks. Lifting the whole knife scatters food and cuts.

test.why: A damp towel grips both surfaces so the board cannot slide.

test.q: A knife falls off the counter. You should

In a sink full of soapy water

grinds a new edge and is done rarely

The steps for any dice are

title: Knife Skills

chapters.title: The Knife and the Grip
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you hold and care for a chef's knife so it does what you want and never what you don't?

story.title: First Day on the Board
story.kicker: Marcus had used a butter knife a hundred times. The eight-inch chef's knife on the board in front of him was something else.
paragraphs: The knives came out of a locked drawer, one per station, handle first. Ms. Okafor set Marcus's knife on his cutting board with the edge facing away from him. Under the board was a damp paper towel. "Push the board," she said. Marcus pushed. It did not slide. "That towel is the first safety rule you will learn today," she said.

Marcus wrapped his whole fist around the handle, the way he held a hammer. Ms. Okafor shook her head and took his hand. She slid his thumb and the side of his first finger up onto the flat of the blade, just in front of the handle. His other three fingers curled around the handle. "That is the pinch grip," she said. "You are holding the blade, not just the handle. Now the knife goes where your hand goes."

Then she gave him a carrot. His left hand went flat on it, fingers stretched out. "Stop," she said. "Tuck them." She showed him: fingertips curled under, knuckles forward, thumb tucked behind. The knife's flat side rested against his knuckles. "The claw. The blade can touch your knuckles all day. It cannot reach your fingertips if they are tucked."

The first cut was slow. The tip of the knife stayed on the board and the handle came down and forward, like a rocking chair. A coin of carrot rolled away. Marcus did it again, and again. Ten slices in, he stopped looking at the knife and started looking at his claw hand. That was when the slices got even.

At the end, Ms. Okafor asked the class to hold up their knives. Nobody did. "Good," she said. "A knife never goes up in the air in this room. It goes on the board, edge away, or it goes to the sink, one at a time, handle first." Marcus set his down, edge toward the wall, and realized his hands were shaking a little. Not from fear. From paying attention.
story.think: Marcus made two mistakes before he cut anything: the hammer grip and the flat hand. Why does each one matter, and what did the fix look like?

lessons.title: Parts of a Chef's Knife
lessons.mainIdea: A chef's knife has six named parts, and each one has a job in a cut.
reading: Pick up a chef's knife by the handle and lay it flat on the board, edge away from you. Look at it from the side. The pointed end is the *tip*. The sharp bottom line running from the tip back to the handle is the *edge*. The back corner of the edge, nearest the handle, is the *heel*. The thick, dull top of the blade is the *spine*.

Where the blade meets the handle, many knives have a thick band of metal called the *bolster*. It adds weight and keeps your hand from sliding forward onto the edge. Behind it is the handle. Some handles are wood, some are plastic; either way, it should feel dry and solid in your hand.

Each part does something. The tip pierces and does fine work like the first cuts on an onion. The middle of the edge does most slicing. The heel is the strongest part; use it for hard things like a squash. The spine is safe to touch, so you can push cut food off the board with the spine, never the edge.

A chef's knife is usually 8 inches long, and that is the one you will use most. A paring knife is a small knife, about 3 to 4 inches, for peeling and small jobs. A serrated knife has teeth and saws through bread and tomatoes. Learn the chef's knife first; the rest follow the same rules.

words.d: the pointed front end of the blade, used for piercing and fine cuts
the sharp bottom line of the blade that does the cutting
the back corner of the edge, nearest the handle; the strongest part for hard foods
the thick, dull top of the blade; safe to touch and push food with
the thick band of metal between blade and handle that stops the hand sliding forward

look.title: Name the Part
look.text: A knife lies on the board. Point A is the very front. Point B is the sharp line along the bottom. Point C is the back corner of that line, near the handle. Point D is the thick top line. Point E is the metal band where blade meets handle. A student wants to split a hard butternut squash. Another wants to sweep chopped onion off the board into a bowl.
look.prompt: Name parts A through E. Which part should each student use, and why?

check.q: Which part of the knife is safe to touch and can push cut food across the board?
check.why: The spine is the dull top of the blade. Pushing with the edge dulls it and can cut you.

check.q: You need to cut through a hard sweet potato. Which part of the edge should do the work?
check.why: The heel is the strongest part of the edge, closest to your hand, and gives the most force.

check.q: What does the bolster do?
choices: Sharpens the edge as you cut
Keeps your hand from sliding forward onto the edge
Holds the knife in the drawer
check.why: The bolster is the thick band between blade and handle. It stops your hand sliding onto the edge.

lessons.title: Sharp Is Safer
lessons.mainIdea: A sharp knife cuts where you aim it; a dull knife slips, and slips are how people get cut.
reading: Picture a dull knife on a tomato. You press down. The skin does not split. You press harder. The blade suddenly skids sideways across the tomato and off the board. That skid is where the edge meets a finger. Now picture a sharp knife: a light pull and the skin opens right where the edge touched.

This is the rule that surprises everyone: a *sharp* knife is safer than a dull one. Sharp means the edge is thin and even, so it bites the food with little force. *Dull* means the edge is rounded or nicked, so you must push hard, and a hard push is a push you cannot control. Most kitchen cuts come from dull knives that slipped.

Test sharpness with paper, not your thumb. Hold a sheet of paper by one corner and draw the knife down through it. A sharp knife slices cleanly. A dull one tears or catches. Never run a finger along the edge to test it. Tell your teacher if a knife is dull; do not just push harder.

A sharp knife still deserves respect. Sharp means every rule matters more, not less: eyes on the blade, claw hand, board that does not slide. The knife does exactly what your hands tell it. Your job is to tell it clearly.

words.d: an edge that is thin and even, so it cuts with little pushing
an edge that is rounded or nicked, so it needs hard pushing and can slip

look.title: Two Knives, One Tomato
look.text: Station 1: the student presses down on a tomato, the skin dents but does not open, and the student leans harder. Station 2: the student pulls the blade lightly across the tomato and the skin splits at once. Both students are using the same kind of knife.
look.prompt: Which knife is dull? Which student is more likely to be cut in the next ten seconds, and exactly what would cause it?

check.q: Why is a dull knife more dangerous than a sharp one?
choices: It needs hard pushing and can slip
check.why: A dull edge needs force. Force you cannot control leads to a slip, and slips cause cuts.

check.q: What is the safe way to test whether a knife is sharp?
choices: Slice a sheet of paper held by its corner
Run your thumb along the edge
Press it into your palm lightly
check.why: A sharp knife slices paper cleanly. Never test an edge with your skin.

check.q: A student finds the knife will not cut a tomato skin. What should the student do?
choices: Tell the teacher the knife is dull
check.why: Pushing harder on a dull edge is how slips happen. Report it and get a sharp knife.

lessons.title: The Right Knife for the Job
lessons.mainIdea: Match the knife to the food: chef's knife for most work, paring for small jobs, serrated for bread and tomatoes.
reading: Three foods sit on the board: a loaf of crusty bread, a strawberry, and a head of cabbage. One knife will not do all three well. The cabbage wants the chef's knife: long, heavy, with a heel that pushes through a dense head. The strawberry wants the *paring knife*: short and light, so you can hull it in your hand with small moves.

The bread wants the *serrated knife*. Its edge has teeth, like a saw. Teeth grip a hard crust and a soft inside without crushing them. Press a smooth chef's knife on crusty bread and the loaf flattens before it cuts. Saw gently with the serrated knife and it opens clean. Serrated also works on tomato skin.

Using the wrong knife is a real mistake with real results. A chef's knife on a strawberry is clumsy and your claw hand has nothing to hold. A paring knife on a cabbage is too short; it gets stuck, you push, and it slips. A serrated knife on an onion shreds instead of slicing. Choose first, then cut.

In our room, most days you will pick up the chef's knife. It slices, dices and minces. Reach for the paring knife only for small, in-hand jobs, and for those, cut away from your body, never toward your thumb.

words.d: a small knife, about 3 to 4 inches, for peeling and small in-hand jobs
a knife with a toothed edge that saws through bread and tomatoes

look.title: Common Kitchen Knives
look.cite: typical blade lengths sold for home kitchens
look.prompt: Which of these would you choose to cut a cabbage in half, and which to hull a strawberry? Use the lengths to explain.

check.q: Which knife cuts crusty bread without crushing it?
check.why: The serrated edge has teeth that saw through the crust instead of pressing it flat.

check.q: A student tries to halve a cabbage with a paring knife. What is likely to happen?
choices: The short blade sticks, the student pushes, and it slips
check.why: A 3-inch blade is too short for a dense head; it sticks, and pushing a stuck blade causes slips.

check.q: You are hulling strawberries. Which knife and which direction?
choices: Paring knife, away from your body
check.why: Small in-hand jobs use the paring knife, and the cut always goes away from your body.

lessons.title: The Pinch Grip
lessons.mainIdea: Pinch the blade in front of the handle with thumb and first finger; the other three fingers hold the handle.
reading: Most people grab a knife like a hammer, all four fingers and the thumb wrapped around the handle. The knife wobbles. Every cut lands a little to the left or right of where you meant. Now try this instead. Set the knife on the board. Put your thumb on one flat side of the blade, just in front of the handle. Put the side of your first finger on the other flat side.

Pinch there. Then curl your last three fingers around the handle. That is the *pinch grip*. Your hand is holding the blade itself, near its balance point, so the knife moves as one piece with your hand. Do not put your first finger on top of the spine and point it down the blade. That looks steady but it gives up control.

Check yourself. Hold the knife with the pinch grip and let your arm hang loose. The knife should feel balanced, not tip-heavy. Your wrist should be straight, not bent. If your knuckles are white, you are squeezing. Squeezing tires the hand and makes cuts jumpy. Hold it firm, not tight.
The pinch grip is the same on a big knife and a small one. It will feel strange for the first ten minutes and feel normal by the end of the week. Every cut in this unit starts here.

words.d: holding the knife with thumb and first finger pinching the blade just in front of the handle
the spot on a knife where it would rest level on your finger; near the bolster

look.title: Three Hands on Three Knives
look.text: Hand 1: all five fingers wrapped around the handle, like a hammer. Hand 2: first finger stretched out along the top of the spine, pointing down the blade. Hand 3: thumb on one side of the blade, first finger on the other, three fingers on the handle, wrist straight, knuckles not white.
look.prompt: Which hand has the pinch grip? Say what will go wrong for each of the other two when the student starts cutting.

check.q: In the pinch grip, where are your thumb and first finger?
choices: On the blade just in front of the handle
Wrapped around the end of the handle
On top of the spine, pointing forward
check.why: Pinching the blade in front of the handle holds the knife at its balance point for control.

check.q: What goes wrong with a hammer grip?
choices: The knife wobbles and cuts land off target
check.why: Holding only the handle lets the blade wobble, so cuts are uneven and less safe.

check.q: Your knuckles are white while you cut. What does that tell you?
check.why: White knuckles mean a tight squeeze. That tires the hand and makes cuts jumpy. Hold firm, not tight.

lessons.title: The Claw Hand
lessons.mainIdea: Curl your fingertips under and lead with your knuckles; the flat of the blade rides against the knuckles, never the tips.
reading: Your knife hand is only half the story. The other hand holds the food, and it is the hand that gets cut. Put a carrot on the board. Now look at your guiding hand. If the fingers are flat and stretched out, the fingertips are right in the blade's path. That is the mistake nearly every beginner makes.

Make a *claw*. Curl all four fingertips under so the knuckles stick out in front. Tuck the thumb back behind the fingers. Rest the fingertips on the carrot; the knuckles are now the closest thing to the knife. Bring the flat side of the blade up against your knuckles. Now cut. The blade slides down along the knuckles and cannot reach the tucked tips.

To take the next slice, walk the claw back a little, keeping the knuckles forward and the thumb tucked. The blade follows the knuckles. How far you walk back sets how thick the slice is. Small steps, thin slices. This is how cooks cut fast without looking at the tips.

Common errors: the thumb creeps out in front; the pinky sticks out sideways; the fingers flatten when the food gets small. Near the end of a carrot, stop and turn the last piece on its side, or set it aside. Nobody needs the last quarter inch enough to cut a fingertip for it.

words.d: the guiding-hand shape: fingertips curled under, knuckles forward, thumb tucked behind
the hand that holds the food steady and sets where the next cut lands

look.title: Spot the Fingertip
look.text: A student is slicing a cucumber. The knife hand has a good pinch grip. On the guiding hand, the first three fingers are curled under, but the thumb is stretched out along the side of the cucumber, ahead of the knuckles, holding it steady. The pinky is lifted off to the side. The cucumber has two inches left.
look.prompt: Find the two problems with the guiding hand. What should the student do with the last two inches?

check.q: In the claw, what part of the guiding hand touches the flat of the blade?
check.why: The knuckles lead. The blade rides against them, and the curled fingertips stay behind them.

check.q: How do you make the next slice thinner?
choices: Walk the claw back a smaller step
check.why: The claw sets where the blade lands. A smaller step back gives a thinner slice.

check.q: The carrot is down to a small end piece. What is the safe choice?
choices: Flatten your hand to hold it
Turn it on its side or set it aside
Hold it with fingertips and cut fast
check.why: Small pieces make the claw collapse. Turn the piece or leave it; a fingertip is worth more than a scrap.

lessons.title: The Rocking Cut
lessons.mainIdea: Keep the tip on the board and rock the handle down and forward; the knife slices instead of chopping.
reading: Watch a beginner chop celery. The knife lifts high and comes straight down, thunk. Pieces fly. The blade lands wherever it lands. Now watch a cook. The tip of the knife barely leaves the board. The handle rises and falls, and the blade slides forward as it drops. Quiet, even, fast. That is the *rocking cut*.

Do it this way. Pinch grip. Claw on the celery. Set the tip of the knife on the board just past the food. Lower the handle so the edge meets the celery, and push slightly forward as it goes down, so the edge slides through rather than pressing. Lift the handle, walk the claw back, and repeat. The tip stays down the whole time.

Why it works: a knife cuts best when the edge moves along the food, like a saw, not straight into it, like a stamp. Rocking gives you that forward slide with almost no lifting. Lifting is what makes cuts land off target and what sends pieces flying.

Slow first. Ten slow, even slices teach more than fifty fast, ragged ones. Speed comes on its own once the motion is in your hand. If pieces are flying or the sound is loud, your tip is leaving the board. Put it back down.

words.d: a slicing motion where the tip stays on the board and the handle rocks down and forward
moving the edge along the food as it cuts, instead of pressing straight down

look.title: Listen to the Cut
look.text: Two students cut celery side by side. From across the room you hear station A: thunk, thunk, thunk, with a pause between each. A piece of celery skitters off the board. Station B is nearly silent, a soft tick-tick-tick, and the pieces stay in a neat pile.
look.prompt: Describe what each student's knife tip is doing. What single change would fix station A?

check.q: In the rocking cut, what does the tip of the knife do?
choices: Stays on or near the board
check.why: The tip stays down and the handle rocks. That keeps every cut landing where you aim.

check.q: Why does the blade slide forward as it comes down?
choices: To push food off the board
Because an edge cuts better moving along the food than pressing straight in
check.why: A knife works like a saw, not a stamp. Forward motion lets the edge slice with less force.

check.q: Celery pieces keep flying off the board. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The tip is leaving the board on each stroke
check.why: Lifting the whole knife and chopping down scatters food. Keep the tip down and rock.

lessons.title: Board and Damp Towel
lessons.mainIdea: Put a damp towel under the board so it cannot slide, and give the board room and light.
reading: A cutting board on a smooth counter slides. Push a knife through an onion and the board shifts an inch. Your claw hand moves with the board, your knife hand does not, and the blade lands somewhere new. The fix costs nothing. Wet a paper towel or dish towel, wring it out, and lay it flat under the board. Push the board now. It stays.

Set up the rest of the station. The board sits square in front of you, not at an angle. Leave a clear space on each side: one for food waiting to be cut, one for food already cut. A bowl for scraps saves trips to the trash. Good light on the board; you must see the edge.

Use a plastic or wood board, never glass or a plate. A knife skids on hard glass, and it dulls the edge in minutes. Check the board is dry on top; a wet board makes food slip. If your board is scarred with deep grooves, ask for another; deep grooves hold bacteria and make the surface uneven.

Separate boards keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat food. Many kitchens color-code: one board for raw chicken, a different one for vegetables. When you finish with raw meat, the board and the knife go straight to the sink before anything else touches them. That is *cross-contamination* stopped at the source.

words.d: a wrung-out cloth or paper towel laid under the cutting board so it cannot slide
germs moving from one food to another, often from raw meat to ready-to-eat food, on a board or knife

look.title: Check the Station
look.text: A station before the lab: a glass cutting board sits at an angle on a dry counter, right at the edge. The overhead light is off and the student is working in the shadow of a cabinet. There is no bowl for scraps. A raw chicken breast is on the board with a tomato right beside it.
look.prompt: List every problem with this station and say what you would change before picking up the knife.

check.q: What is the damp towel under the board for?
choices: To keep the board from sliding
check.why: A wrung-out towel grips both the counter and the board. A board that slides sends cuts off target.

check.q: Why should you not cut on a glass board or a plate?
choices: The knife skids on it and the edge dulls fast
check.why: A hard glass surface makes the blade skid and rounds off the edge within minutes.

check.q: You just cut raw chicken on a board. What happens next?
choices: Wipe the board and slice the salad on it
Flip the board over and keep going
Rinse the knife under cold water and reuse it
Board and knife go to the sink before anything else touches them
check.why: Raw meat juices carry bacteria. The board and knife must be washed before they touch ready-to-eat food.

lessons.title: Carrying and Passing a Knife
lessons.mainIdea: Carry a knife pointed down at your side, say what you are doing, and set it down for the next person instead of handing it over.
reading: Someone needs to get past you with a knife on the way to the sink. Picture the worst version: the knife held out in front, edge up, in a crowded room. Now the right version. The blade points straight down at your side, edge facing behind you, your arm straight. You walk, never run, and you say clearly, "Knife, behind you," as you pass.

Never hand a knife to another person blade-first, and really, avoid handing it at all. Set it down on the board with the edge facing away and let the other person pick it up. If you must hand it over, hold the spine with the handle toward them, wait until they say "got it," then let go. One knife at a time. Never toss.

A knife on the counter is a knife that can fall. Keep it back from the edge. Never leave one in a sink full of water where a hand reaching for a plate finds it edge-first. If a knife does fall, do not try to catch it. Step back, let it land, then pick it up by the handle. A dropped knife is cheap; a caught one is a trip to the nurse.
Eyes on the knife whenever it is in your hand. If you need to talk to someone, look at someone, or reach for something, put the knife down first. Cuts happen in the second the eyes leave the blade.

words.d: carrying a knife with the blade straight down at your side, edge facing back
saying "knife" or "behind you" so people know where the blade is

look.title: Four Ways to Move a Knife
look.text: Scene 1: a student walks to the sink with the knife pointing down at the side, saying "knife, behind you." Scene 2: a student hands a knife across the table, blade-first, to a partner who is looking the other way. Scene 3: a student sets the knife on the board, edge away, and says "your turn." Scene 4: a knife slips off the counter and a student lunges to catch it.
look.prompt: Rank the scenes from safest to most dangerous and say what should have happened in the two worst ones.

check.q: How do you carry a knife across the room?
choices: Blade down at your side, and say "knife"
Held out in front so people see it
check.why: Point down at your side keeps the edge away from everyone, and calling out warns them.

check.q: A knife slips off the counter. What do you do?
choices: Step back and let it fall
check.why: Never try to catch a falling knife. Step back, let it land, then pick it up by the handle.

check.q: What is the best way to give a partner the knife?
choices: Set it on the board, edge away, and let them pick it up
Hold it in the sink water for them
check.why: Setting it down removes the hand-off entirely. If you must hand it, spine held, handle toward them, wait for "got it."

lessons.title: Washing a Knife
lessons.mainIdea: Wash a knife by hand right away, edge away from your fingers, and dry it before it goes anywhere.
reading: The lab is over and the sink is full of soapy water. Someone drops the knife in with the bowls. Ten minutes later a hand goes into the water for a spoon. This is the most common knife injury outside of cutting. The rule: a knife never goes into a full sink. Wash it right away, by itself, and put it away.

Here is the method. Hold the handle with the edge facing away from your hand. With a soapy sponge or cloth in the other hand, wipe from the spine side down toward the edge, and from the heel toward the tip, keeping the cloth on the flat sides. Never wrap the cloth around the edge and pull. Rinse under running water, edge away.

Dry it at once with a clean towel, again flat side to flat side, edge away. A wet knife rusts and a wet handle grows bacteria. Then it goes straight to its storage spot. Do not put a good knife in the dishwasher: the heat and the tumbling bang the edge against racks and dull it, and the handle can crack.

If the knife touched raw meat, wash it before it touches anything else, with hot soapy water, and then sanitize the board as your teacher directs. Wash your hands for 20 seconds after handling raw meat too, before the next task.

words.d: to kill germs on a clean surface, after washing, with heat or an approved solution
washing a knife alone with a cloth on the flat sides, edge away, instead of in a sink or dishwasher

look.title: The Sink After the Lab
look.text: The sink has six inches of soapy water with bowls, spoons and a spatula in it. A chef's knife is at the bottom, point up. A student reaches in for a measuring cup. Another student has just finished cutting raw chicken and has set the knife on the counter to go wash hands first.
look.prompt: What should the first student have done with the knife? What is the right order for the second student: hands or knife first, and why?

check.q: Where should a knife never go?
choices: In a sink full of water
check.why: A knife hidden in water is found edge-first by the next hand. Wash it alone, right away.

check.q: When you wipe the blade with a cloth, which way does the cloth move?
choices: Wrapped around the edge, pulled tip to heel
On the flat sides, spine toward edge, edge facing away
check.why: Keep the cloth on the flat sides and move toward the edge, never along it or around it.

check.q: Why not put a chef's knife in the dishwasher?
choices: The tumbling and heat dull the edge and can crack the handle
check.why: Banging against racks dulls an edge, and hot cycles damage handles. Hand wash and dry.

lessons.title: Storing Knives
lessons.mainIdea: Store a knife where the edge is protected and no hand can find it by accident: block, magnetic strip or a guard in a drawer.
reading: Open a messy drawer and feel around for a spatula. If a bare knife is loose in there, your fingers find the edge before your eyes do. Loose knives in a drawer also bang against other tools and dull. A knife needs a home where the edge touches nothing and nobody reaches in blind.

Three good homes. A *knife block* is a wooden stand with slots; slide the knife in spine-down so the edge does not scrape the wood. A *magnetic strip* on the wall holds the flat of the blade; put the spine on first and roll the edge away from the strip when taking it off. A *blade guard* is a plastic sleeve over the edge for a knife that must live in a drawer.

In our room the knives live in a locked drawer, counted out and counted back in. Before the drawer closes, every knife is washed, dry, and in its guard. A wet knife stored away rusts at the edge, and rust makes a dull, uneven blade. A missing knife stops the whole class until it is found.

Storage is also the moment to check the knife. Look at the edge for nicks. Look at the handle for cracks or looseness. A loose handle can twist during a cut. Report problems now, not next time you are halfway through an onion.

words.d: a wooden stand with slots that holds knives with the edge protected
a wall-mounted magnet that holds knives by the flat of the blade
a plastic sleeve that covers the edge of a knife stored in a drawer

look.title: Where Does It Go?
look.text: Kitchen A has a wooden block on the counter. Kitchen B has a drawer full of loose spatulas, whisks and one bare chef's knife. Kitchen C has a magnetic strip on the wall above the stove. Kitchen D has a drawer where each knife wears a plastic sleeve.
look.prompt: Which kitchen is unsafe, and what is the cheapest fix? For the block and the strip, describe how the knife goes in and comes out without touching the edge.

check.q: Why is a bare knife loose in a drawer dangerous?
choices: Fingers find the edge before eyes do
check.why: Reaching blind into a drawer with a bare edge is how hands get cut. Guard it or store it elsewhere.

check.q: How do you slide a knife into a wooden block?
choices: Spine down so the edge does not scrape
check.why: Sliding it spine-down keeps the edge off the wood, so the block does not dull it.

check.q: Before a knife goes into the locked drawer, it must be
choices: washed, dry and in its guard
check.why: Dry prevents rust, the guard protects the edge and the next hand. Washed is never optional.

lessons.title: Honing and Sharpening
lessons.mainIdea: Honing straightens the edge often; sharpening grinds a new edge rarely, and an adult does it.
reading: A knife that cut fine last week now drags on a tomato. The edge has not worn away; it has bent. Under a magnifier, the thin edge of a knife folds slightly to one side with use. *Honing* pushes it straight again. A honing steel is a long rod with a handle. Cooks hone before nearly every use.

You will see your teacher hone, and you may be taught to do it with supervision. The steel is held point-down on a towel on the counter. The knife's edge is drawn down the steel at a shallow angle, heel to tip, first one side, then the other, lightly, a few strokes each. Then the knife is wiped clean, because honing leaves tiny metal dust.

*Sharpening* is different. It grinds away metal to make a new edge. It happens a few times a year on a whetstone or with a sharpening tool. Sharpening is an adult's job in our kitchen; a stone used wrong ruins a knife. Your job is to notice: if a knife still drags after honing, tell your teacher it needs sharpening.

Between honing and sharpening sits everyday care: cut on wood or plastic, never glass; never scrape with the edge; never use the knife to open cans or pry lids. Every one of those bends or chips an edge, and then you are back to a dull knife and a slip waiting to happen.

words.d: straightening a bent edge on a steel rod, done often, removing almost no metal
grinding away metal on a stone or tool to form a new edge, done rarely, by an adult
a long rod with a handle that the edge is drawn along to straighten it

look.title: Knife Care Calendar (example)
look.cite: example care schedule for a busy home kitchen
look.prompt: Which two jobs happen every time you use the knife? Why is sharpening so much less often than honing?

check.q: What does honing do to a knife's edge?
check.why: Honing pushes a folded edge back straight. It removes almost no metal and is done often.

check.q: A knife still drags on a tomato right after honing. What should you do?
choices: Use it on glass to clean the edge
Tell the teacher it needs sharpening
check.why: If honing does not fix it, the edge is worn. Sharpening grinds a new one and is an adult's job.

check.q: Which everyday habit dulls or chips an edge?
choices: Prying a lid with the tip
check.why: A knife tip is for cutting, not prying. Prying bends or snaps the thin edge.

review.q: Which part of the knife is the strongest and best for a hard squash?
review.why: The heel is the back of the edge nearest the hand and delivers the most force.

review.q: A student presses harder and harder on a tomato and the blade skids. What is the root cause?
review.why: A dull edge needs force, and force turns into slips. Sharp knives cut where you aim.

review.q: In the pinch grip, the last three fingers are
review.why: Thumb and first finger pinch the blade; the other three fingers wrap the handle.

review.q: In the claw, the part of the guiding hand closest to the blade is
review.why: Knuckles lead and the blade rides against them. Tucked tips stay out of the path.

review.q: In the rocking cut, what stays on the board?
review.why: The tip stays down and the handle rocks. Lifting the whole knife scatters food and cuts.

review.q: The board keeps sliding. The fix is
choices: a plate instead of a board
leaning on the board with your elbow
review.why: A wrung-out towel under the board grips the counter. A sliding board sends cuts off target.

review.q: The right way to walk a knife to the sink is
choices: blade forward so people see it
blade down at your side, calling "knife"
review.why: Point down, edge back, and say what you are doing. Never run, never toss.

review.q: After washing, a knife should be
choices: left in the sink to soak
dried right away and stored with the edge protected
put in the dishwasher for sanitizing
set on the counter edge to dry
review.why: Dry prevents rust; a block, strip or guard protects the edge and the next hand.

chapters.title: The Classic Cuts
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do cooks cut food into named shapes and sizes, and how do you make each one?

story.title: Salsa Night, Four Cuts
story.kicker: One bowl of salsa needed an onion, a tomato, two cloves of garlic and a handful of cilantro. Each one wanted a different cut.
paragraphs: The recipe card on Jada's station said: 1 onion, small dice. 2 tomatoes, medium dice. 2 cloves garlic, minced. Cilantro, chopped. Lime juice and salt. Four ingredients, four different words. Jada looked at her partner Tomas. "They are all just chopping," he said. Ms. Okafor, walking past, said, "Then why did I write four different words?"

Jada started with the onion. She cut it in half through the root, peeled it, and laid a half flat. Horizontal cuts toward the root, not through it. Then vertical cuts, a quarter inch apart. Then across. Little quarter-inch cubes fell in a pile. The root end held the whole thing together until the last cut. "That is the trick," she said. "The root is the handle."

Tomas took the tomato. He tried the same cuts but the tomato squished and the seeds ran out. Ms. Okafor showed him: slice off the top, cut it into thick slabs with a gentle sawing motion, stack the slabs, cut strips, cut across. Half-inch cubes. Bigger than the onion, because a tomato that size still had some bite to it.

The garlic was tiny. Jada smashed a clove under the flat of the blade with the heel of her hand, and the peel fell off. Then she rocked the knife over it again and again, keeping the tip down, until the pieces were smaller than a grain of rice. "Mince," said Ms. Okafor. "Small enough to melt into everything."

Tomas rolled the cilantro leaves into a tight bundle and sliced across into thin ribbons. When they stirred the bowl, the pieces looked like they belonged together: small onion, bigger tomato, garlic you could not see but could taste, green ribbons on top. "Four cuts," Tomas said. "Four different jobs," said Ms. Okafor. "That is why they have names."
story.think: Each ingredient in the salsa got a different cut. Pick two of them and explain why that size made sense for that food in that bowl.

lessons.title: Slice and Rough Chop
lessons.mainIdea: A slice is a flat, even piece; a rough chop is quick, uneven pieces for food that will be blended or strained.
reading: Put a cucumber on the board. Claw hand on it, pinch grip on the knife, tip down. Rock the knife through, walk the claw back a small step, rock again. Each piece that falls is a *slice*: a flat piece with two parallel faces. Slices are for sandwiches, salads, stir-fry, anywhere the piece will be seen or needs to cook flat in a pan.

Slices should match. If one is a quarter inch and the next is half an inch, they will not cook alike. The claw controls it: same step back, same slice. Beginners rush and the claw takes big, uneven steps. Slow down until every slice is a twin of the last, then speed up.

A *rough chop* is the opposite idea. You are cutting an onion for a soup that will be blended, or carrots for a stock that will be strained. Nobody will see the pieces. Cut the food into chunks about an inch across, fast, without worrying about a perfect shape. Rough chop is not sloppy. It is a real cut with a purpose: speed, where looks do not matter.

Choose by asking: will anyone see or bite this piece? If yes, slice or dice it evenly. If it is going into a blender or a strainer, rough chop and move on. Cooks save their careful cuts for where they count.

words.d: a flat, even piece with two parallel faces, cut with the rocking motion
quick, uneven chunks about an inch across, for food that will be blended or strained

look.title: Slice It or Chop It?
look.text: Four jobs: cucumber for a salad that goes on the table; an onion for a soup that will be blended smooth; carrots and celery for a chicken stock that will be strained and thrown out; mushrooms for a pizza topping.
look.prompt: For each job, choose slice or rough chop and give the reason in one sentence.

check.q: What makes a good slice?
choices: It is as thin as paper
It is cut with the tip only
It matches the slices before it
check.why: Even slices cook alike. The claw's step back controls the thickness.

check.q: When is a rough chop the right choice?
choices: Food that will be blended or strained
A carrot coin for a stir-fry
check.why: Rough chop is for food nobody will see or bite as a piece. It trades neatness for speed.

check.q: Your cucumber slices are all different thicknesses. What is the fix?
choices: Walk the claw back the same small step each time
check.why: The guiding hand sets slice thickness. Same step, same slice.

lessons.title: Dice, Three Sizes
lessons.mainIdea: Dice means cubes: small is 1/4 inch, medium 1/2 inch, large 3/4 inch, and the recipe tells you which.
reading: Look at the salsa recipe: onion, small dice. Tomato, medium dice. A *dice* is a cube, all sides the same. The word tells you the shape; the size word tells you how big. In most American kitchens, *small dice* is a 1/4-inch cube, *medium dice* is 1/2 inch, and *large dice* is 3/4 inch. Ruler out; those numbers are real.

Every dice is made the same way, no matter the size. First, cut the food into flat slabs as thick as the dice you want. Second, stack the slabs and cut them into sticks as wide as the dice. Third, turn the sticks and cut across, so each cut drops a cube. Slabs, sticks, cubes. Three steps, every time.

Try it on a potato for a medium dice. Cut a thin slice off one side so the potato sits flat and does not roll. Cut 1/2-inch slabs. Stack two or three slabs and cut 1/2-inch sticks. Turn the sticks and cut across every 1/2 inch. If your cubes are rectangles, one of the three steps used a different measurement.

Which size? Small dice for things that should blend in: onion in salsa, celery in tuna salad. Medium dice for soups and stews where you want to see and bite the piece. Large dice for roasting, where small pieces would burn before big ones finished. The recipe will say; when it does not, match the other ingredients.

words.d: to cut into cubes with all sides the same length
a 1/4-inch cube
a 1/2-inch cube
a 3/4-inch cube

look.title: Dice Sizes
look.cite: standard dice sizes taught in American culinary programs
look.prompt: A recipe says 'potatoes, large dice.' Draw a square that size. How many small-dice cubes would fit along one edge of it?

check.q: A medium dice is a cube that measures
check.why: Small is 1/4 inch, medium is 1/2 inch, large is 3/4 inch.

check.q: What is the order of steps for any dice?
check.why: Slabs first, stack them into sticks, then cut across the sticks to drop cubes.

check.q: Your 'cubes' came out as long rectangles. What went wrong?
choices: One of the three cuts used a different width than the others
check.why: A cube needs all three cuts at the same measurement. One different width makes rectangles.

lessons.title: Even Pieces Cook Evenly
lessons.mainIdea: Same-size pieces finish at the same time; mixed sizes give you burnt bits and raw bits in one pan.
reading: Picture a tray of roasted potatoes. Some pieces are 1/4 inch, some are a full inch. Pull the tray at twenty minutes: the small pieces are black at the edges and the big ones are still hard in the middle. There was no right moment to take them out. That is the whole reason cuts have sizes.

Heat moves into food from the outside in. A small piece has a short trip to its center; a big piece has a long one. In the same pan at the same heat, the small piece is done first. If every piece is the same size, every piece is done at the same moment, and the cook can pull the pan without guessing.

This is also a safety point. Ground meat must reach 160 °F all the way through and poultry 165 °F. A big chunk in a pan of small ones can still be under temperature when the small ones look done. Even sizes mean the thermometer reading in one piece tells the truth about all of them.

So when a recipe says 1/2-inch dice, it is not being fussy. It is telling you how long the food will take and asking you to make the pieces agree. Before the food goes in the pan, look at the pile. If one piece stands out as bigger, cut it again.

words.d: pieces all the same size so they cook at the same rate
the point at which food is cooked through; for meat, a safe internal temperature

look.title: Safe Internal Temperatures
rows: whole cuts of beef and pork (then rest 3 min)
look.prompt: A pan of chicken pieces has one chunk twice the size of the rest. The thermometer reads 165 °F in a small piece. Can you serve the big one? Why not?

check.q: Why do cooks cut vegetables to one size before roasting?
choices: So they take up less room
So they are easier to count
So every piece finishes cooking at the same time
check.why: Heat travels from outside in. Same size means same cooking time for every piece.

check.q: A tray of mixed-size potatoes comes out of the oven. What do you expect?
choices: Small pieces burnt, big pieces raw inside
Big pieces burnt, small pieces raw
check.why: Small pieces finish first and burn while big pieces are still hard in the center.

check.q: Ground beef patties of different thickness are on the grill. The thin one reads 160 °F. The thick one is
choices: also done, because they started together
probably under 160 °F and needs its own reading
check.why: A thicker piece has farther for heat to travel. Every piece that differs needs its own thermometer check; ground beef is 160 °F.

lessons.title: Mince
lessons.mainIdea: Mince means cut as small as you can, so the food melts into the dish and spreads its flavor everywhere.
reading: Bite into a salad and hit a raw chunk of garlic the size of a pea. Too strong, and nobody else got any. Now imagine the same clove cut so fine that every bite has a trace. That is what *mince* is for: pieces smaller than a grain of rice, so a strong flavor spreads evenly through a dish.

Minced garlic, minced ginger, minced herbs, minced shallot. The method starts with a rough chop, then keeps going. Gather the pieces into a small pile. Put the tip of the knife on the board past the pile and rest your free hand flat on the spine near the tip, fingers well back from the edge. Rock the handle up and down, sweeping across the pile.

Every few rocks, stop, scrape the pile back together with the spine of the knife, not the edge, and go again. Keep going until nothing is bigger than a rice grain. A common mistake is to lift the tip and chop; pieces scatter, and you spend more time gathering than cutting. Tip stays down, hand on the spine.

Mince is small, but it is not mush. If the pile turns into paste, you have over-worked it or pressed too hard. Light strokes. For garlic and ginger, cooks sometimes want a paste on purpose, and they add a pinch of salt and drag the flat of the blade over it. That is a different tool: ask before you do it.

words.d: to cut into pieces smaller than a grain of rice so flavor spreads through the dish
to sweep cut pieces back into a pile with the spine of the knife between rounds of cutting

look.title: Hand on the Spine
look.text: A student is mincing parsley. The knife tip is on the board. The free hand is resting flat on top of the blade near the tip, with all four fingers stretched out over the spine and the fingertips hanging an inch past the edge on the far side. The student rocks the handle quickly.
look.prompt: The hand on the spine is a real technique, but something here is wrong. What is it, and how far back should the fingers be?

check.q: How small is a mince?
choices: Smaller than a grain of rice
check.why: Mince is the finest cut, so a strong flavor like garlic spreads through every bite.

check.q: What do you use to sweep the pile back together between rounds?
choices: Your bare fingers under the blade
check.why: The spine is dull and safe. Scraping with the edge dulls it and risks fingers.

check.q: While mincing, pieces keep flying off the board. What should change?
choices: Keep the tip on the board and rock instead of lifting
check.why: Lifting and chopping scatters food. The rocking motion with the tip down keeps the pile together.

lessons.title: Julienne
lessons.mainIdea: Julienne is matchsticks: 1/8 inch by 1/8 inch, about 2 inches long, made from thin slabs stacked and cut into strips.
reading: A carrot slaw, a stir-fry, a garnish on top of a soup: these want long thin sticks that cook fast and look neat. That cut is *julienne*, and the standard size is 1/8 inch by 1/8 inch, about 2 inches long. Think of a matchstick. It is a fine cut and takes patience, so start with a carrot, which is firm and forgiving.

Peel the carrot. Cut it into 2-inch lengths. Cut a thin slice off one side of each length so it sits flat and does not roll; a rolling carrot is a slipping carrot. Now cut the piece lengthwise into slabs 1/8 inch thick. Stack two or three slabs, no more, or the stack shifts. Cut the stack lengthwise into 1/8-inch strips. Matchsticks.

The claw matters more here than anywhere. The cuts are thin and close together, so the knuckles must lead and the steps back must be tiny. Keep the knife blade upright, not tilted, or your slabs will be wedges: thick on one side, thin on the other. Look at your cut face after the first slab and fix your angle before cutting more.

Julienne connects to another cut. Line up your matchsticks and cut across them every 1/8 inch, and you get tiny 1/8-inch cubes. Cooks call that *brunoise*. It is the same slabs-sticks-cubes idea as a dice, just very small. Julienne is dice stopped one step early.

words.d: matchstick strips, 1/8 inch by 1/8 inch and about 2 inches long
tiny 1/8-inch cubes made by cutting across julienne strips
a thin slice taken off a round food so it sits steady on the board

look.title: Cut Sizes Side by Side
look.cite: standard knife-cut dimensions used in culinary training
look.prompt: How many julienne widths fit across one medium dice? What single extra step turns julienne into brunoise?

check.q: What is the standard size of a julienne strip?
choices: 1/8 inch by 1/8 inch, about 2 inches long
check.why: Julienne is a matchstick: 1/8 by 1/8 inch, about 2 inches long.

check.q: Why cut a flat side on the carrot before making slabs?
choices: So it does not roll under the knife
check.why: A round food rolls, and a rolling food slips. A flat side keeps it steady.

check.q: Your slabs are thick on one side and thin on the other. Why?
choices: The blade was tilted instead of upright
check.why: A tilted blade cuts wedges. Keep the blade straight up and down and check the first slab.

lessons.title: Chiffonade
lessons.mainIdea: Chiffonade is thin ribbons of leafy herbs or greens, made by stacking, rolling tight and slicing across the roll.
reading: A handful of basil leaves for a pasta, or spinach for a soup. Chop them with a rocking mince and they bruise and go dark. Instead, stack the leaves, largest on the bottom, six to eight at a time. Roll the stack up tightly from one side like a small cigar. Hold the roll with the claw and slice across it very thinly. The roll falls apart into fine green ribbons. That is *chiffonade*.

The word is French and means "made of rags," which tells you the shape: soft, thin strips. It works for any flat leaf: basil, mint, sage, spinach, kale with the stem cut out, lettuce for a salad. Take out thick stems first; a stem in the roll makes a hard lump that will not slice.

Two mistakes are common. Loose roll: the leaves slide as you cut and you get uneven, ragged strips. Roll tight and hold the roll firmly with the claw. Dull knife: a dull edge crushes the leaves instead of slicing them, and the cut edges turn black within minutes. Herbs show a dull knife faster than any other food.

Cut chiffonade last, just before serving, because the thin ribbons wilt and darken quickly. Fluff the ribbons apart with your fingers and scatter them on top. The whole point is a fresh green look and a bright taste in every bite.

words.d: thin ribbons of leafy herbs or greens, made by rolling the leaves and slicing across the roll
to crush a leaf so it darkens and loses flavor, usually from a dull knife or rough chopping

look.title: Basil in Three Stations
look.text: Station 1: basil leaves are chopped with a fast rocking motion and the pieces are dark and wet. Station 2: leaves are stacked, rolled loosely, and the strips come out in ragged, different widths. Station 3: leaves are stacked, rolled tight, sliced thin, and fluffed into bright green ribbons.
look.prompt: Name the cut at station 3. What went wrong at stations 1 and 2, and what would fix each?

check.q: What is the order for a chiffonade?
check.why: Stack the leaves, roll them tightly, hold the roll with the claw and slice thinly across it.

check.q: Why does a dull knife matter more for herbs than for a carrot?
choices: A dull edge crushes the leaves and they turn dark fast
Carrots do not need a knife
check.why: Crushed leaf cells darken and lose flavor. A sharp slice keeps ribbons green.

check.q: When should chiffonade be cut?
choices: Right after washing, then stored in water
check.why: Thin ribbons wilt and darken quickly, so cut them last and scatter them on top.

lessons.title: Dicing an Onion
lessons.mainIdea: Halve through the root, keep the root on, cut toward it twice, then across; the root holds the onion together.
reading: An onion is the cut cooks practice most, and the root end is the secret. Cut the onion in half from the stem end down through the root. Peel each half, leaving the root attached. Cut off the dry stem end only. Lay a half flat side down with the root pointing away from your knife hand, to the side.

First cuts: horizontal. Hold the top of the onion with your claw hand flat and pressing down, fingers well back. Slide the knife into the side, parallel to the board, and cut toward the root without cutting through it. Two or three of these for a medium dice, more for small. Some cooks skip this step and get slightly bigger pieces; that is fine for a start.

Second cuts: vertical, from stem end toward the root, again stopping before the root. Space them the width of the dice you want: 1/4 inch for small, 1/2 inch for medium. Keep the tip pointed at the root so the cuts fan out slightly. Third cuts: turn the knife and cut across, walking the claw back the same width. Cubes fall away. The root end is the last piece; throw it out.

Onions make eyes water because cutting releases a gas. A sharp knife crushes fewer cells and releases less. Chilling the onion first helps too. Common mistakes: cutting the root off first, so the layers slide apart; horizontal cuts with the claw hand in the blade's path; and pushing straight down instead of slicing, which crushes and squeaks.

words.d: the hairy bottom of the onion that holds the layers together while you cut
a cut made with the blade parallel to the board, toward the root but not through it

look.title: Order the Onion
look.text: Six steps, out of order: (a) cut across to drop cubes; (b) cut in half through the root; (c) vertical cuts toward the root, not through it; (d) peel, leaving the root on; (e) horizontal cuts toward the root with the claw hand flat on top; (f) lay the half flat, root to the side.
look.prompt: Put the steps in order. Which step do some cooks skip, and what changes if they do?

check.q: Why do you leave the root end on the onion while dicing?
choices: It makes the onion sit higher
It holds the layers together until the last cut
It keeps your eyes from watering
check.why: The root is the handle. Cut it off first and the layers slide apart under the knife.

check.q: In which direction do the horizontal cuts go?
choices: Through the root, all the way
Toward the root, stopping before it
check.why: All the first cuts run toward the root and stop short of it, so the onion stays whole.

check.q: Your diced onion fell apart into loose rings before you cut across. Most likely you
choices: cut the root off at the start
made the vertical cuts too close
check.why: Without the root, nothing holds the layers. Keep it on until the very last cut.

lessons.title: Mincing Garlic
lessons.mainIdea: Smash the clove under the flat of the blade to loosen the peel, slice, then rock into a fine mince.
reading: Break a clove off the head of garlic. Set it on the board. Lay the flat side of the chef's knife on top of it, edge facing away from you, and press down with the heel of your hand on the flat of the blade, not on the edge. The clove cracks and the papery skin loosens. Peel it off. Cut off the hard root tip.

Now slice the clove thin lengthwise, then turn the slices and cut them into thin strips. Gather into a pile. Tip of the knife on the board, free hand flat on the spine near the tip, fingers back. Rock through the pile, gather with the spine, rock again, until nothing is bigger than a grain of rice.

The smash is where beginners get hurt. Two rules. The edge faces away from you and your hand presses the flat of the blade, never anywhere near the edge. And press, do not slap; a hard slap can bounce the blade. If you need more force for a big clove, use the heel of your hand and lean in.

Garlic burns fast in a hot pan because the pieces are so small. Cooks add minced garlic near the end or on lower heat, and it turns golden, not brown. Brown garlic is bitter. That is a cooking fact you will meet again, and the reason cooks sometimes leave garlic in bigger pieces when it will cook for a long time.

words.d: pressing a garlic clove under the flat of the blade with the heel of the hand to loosen the peel
one section of a head of garlic

look.title: The Smash, Two Ways
look.text: Student A lays the knife flat on a clove, edge pointing toward their own body, and slaps the blade hard with an open palm. Student B lays the knife flat on a clove, edge facing away, and presses down steadily on the flat of the blade with the heel of the hand, leaning in until the clove cracks.
look.prompt: Find two dangers in Student A's method. Then write the steps that come after the smash.

check.q: When smashing a clove, which way does the edge face?
check.why: Edge away, hand on the flat of the blade, steady press. That keeps the edge from ever meeting your hand.

check.q: What does the smash accomplish?
choices: It loosens the peel so it slides off
check.why: Cracking the clove breaks the papery skin free, which is much faster than peeling by hand.

check.q: Minced garlic went dark brown and bitter in the pan. Why?
choices: The mince was too small for a hot pan and burned
check.why: Tiny pieces burn fast. Add minced garlic late or on lower heat until golden.

lessons.title: Chiffonade of Basil
lessons.mainIdea: Stack six to eight leaves, roll them tight, slice thin across the roll, and fluff the ribbons just before serving.
reading: Rinse the basil and pat it fully dry; wet leaves stick and slip. Pinch off the leaves from the stems. Pick out six to eight of the biggest and stack them, largest on the bottom, all facing the same way. Small leaves can go in the middle of the stack. Line up the stems at one end.

Starting from one long side, roll the stack tightly into a tube. Hold the tube with your claw hand, knuckles forward, thumb tucked. Use the rocking motion and slice across the tube in thin strips, about 1/8 inch, walking the claw back a tiny step each time. Do not press; let the sharp edge do it.

Unroll a piece with your fingers. You should see long, even ribbons. If they are ragged, the roll was loose or the knife was dull. If they are dark at the edges, the knife was dull or the leaves were bruised by pressing. Fix the cause before cutting the next stack.

Fluff the pile apart and scatter it on the dish right away. In a lab with one bunch of basil for four stations, you will get about ten leaves each. Practice the roll on lettuce first if you want; it is cheap and behaves the same way. Then the basil goes on the pasta and looks like it came from a restaurant.

words.d: leaves laid on top of each other, largest on the bottom, before rolling
one thin strip of leaf that falls from a sliced chiffonade roll

look.title: Ten Leaves, One Roll
look.text: You have ten basil leaves, still wet from rinsing, two with thick stems attached. A partner suggests chopping them all at once with a fast rocking motion to save time. The pasta will be served in fifteen minutes.
look.prompt: Write the steps you would actually take, in order, starting with the wet leaves. When do you cut, and why not now?

check.q: Why pat the basil dry before rolling?
choices: Wet leaves stick and slip during the cut
check.why: Wet leaves slide in the roll and on the board, making ragged, uneven ribbons.

check.q: Ribbons come out ragged and uneven. The most likely cause is
choices: too many leaves in the stack
a loose roll or a dull knife
check.why: A loose roll shifts under the blade and a dull edge tears. Roll tight and use a sharp knife.

check.q: When do the ribbons go on the pasta?
choices: An hour ahead, so they soften
check.why: Thin ribbons wilt and darken in minutes. Cut last and scatter at once.

lessons.title: Salsa Prep, Start to Finish
lessons.mainIdea: A practical is one recipe done in order: station set up, cuts in the right sizes, board and knife clean at the end.
reading: The practical is a timed lab: one recipe, four cuts, you at the board. The recipe is fresh salsa. One small onion, small dice. Two tomatoes, medium dice. Two cloves garlic, minced. A small handful of cilantro, chiffonade or rough chop. Juice of one lime, a pinch of salt. Stir. Nothing gets cooked, so every cut will be seen and tasted.

Set up first: damp towel under the board, scrap bowl, one bowl for the finished salsa, knife on the board edge away. Wash hands 20 seconds. Then work from the cut that keeps best to the one that fades fastest. Onion first. Then tomato: cut off the top, slabs with a gentle sawing motion so the seeds stay in, stack, sticks, 1/2-inch cubes. Then garlic, smashed and minced.

Cilantro last. Stack, roll, slice, or rough chop if the recipe allows; ask which. Squeeze the lime, add salt, stir gently so the tomato does not turn to mush. Taste with a clean spoon, once, then set the spoon in the sink. Then, before anyone tastes your salsa, the knife is washed, dried and back in its guard, and the board is in the sink.

The clock matters, but not the way beginners think. Fast, ragged cuts lose more points than slow, even ones. Plan your order, keep the tip down, keep the claw tucked, and the speed will come. Students who finish early with a sloppy board score lower than students who finish on time with a clean one.

words.d: a hands-on test where you do the skill at the board while a teacher watches
cutting the ingredient that keeps best first and the one that fades fastest last

choices: Cilantro, because the leaves fade fastest

choices: The on-time one, for even cuts and a clean station
check.why: Speed counts less than correct sizes, safe technique and a clean finish.

lessons.title: How the Practical Is Graded
lessons.mainIdea: The grade comes from safety, correct sizes, evenness, and cleanup; speed is last on the list.
reading: A rubric is a scoring sheet that tells you what the teacher will look for before you start. For the knife practical it has four parts. Safety: pinch grip, claw, tip down, damp towel, knife carried and stored right. Accuracy: is the small dice actually 1/4 inch, the medium 1/2 inch, the mince rice-sized? Evenness: do the pieces match each other? Cleanup: knife washed and dried, board to the sink, station wiped.

Safety is checked all the time, not just at the end. A flat guiding hand, even once, costs points, because the teacher is grading the habit, not the luck. A knife left in the sink or handed blade-first can end the practical on the spot. Nobody has to be hurt for it to count; the unsafe move is the mistake.

Accuracy is measured with a ruler. The teacher picks up a few cubes from your pile and lays them on a ruler. 1/4 inch is 1/4 inch. Evenness is judged by eye: a pile of cubes that look like twins scores high, a pile with two big chunks in it scores lower, even if the average size is right. Cut the big ones again before you finish.

Cleanup is the part students forget when the clock is loud. It is a quarter of the grade for a reason: in a real kitchen, a dirty board and a wet knife left out are the next person's accident. Finish the cut, finish the clean, then say "done." That is the whole practical, and it is the whole job.

words.d: a scoring sheet that lists what will be judged and how many points each part is worth
whether each cut is the size the recipe named, checked with a ruler
whether the pieces in a pile match each other in size

check.q: Which part of the rubric is worth the most?
check.why: Safe habits are graded throughout. An unsafe move counts even when no one is hurt.

check.q: How does the teacher check accuracy?
choices: By laying a few cubes on a ruler
check.why: Accuracy means the named size. A ruler shows whether a small dice is really 1/4 inch.

check.q: A pile of medium dice has two big chunks in it. Before saying done, you should

leave them; the average is right

So every piece finishes cooking at the same time

choices: left on until the last cut to hold the layers
review.why: The root holds the onion together through the horizontal and vertical cuts.

review.why: Edge away, hand on the flat, steady press. The edge never points at any part of you.
